**The Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, the Directive is repealed with effect from that same day, and Directive 2006/42/EC is therefore still in force today.**

- **General date of application:** Article 54 states that the Regulation "shall apply from 20 January 2027" ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02023R1230-20260529/art_54)).
- **Repeal of the Directive:** Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from the same day, under Articles 54 and 51 ([standardsdrift.com](https://standardsdrift.com/standards/machinery-regulation/)).
- **Effect of the corrigendum:** The text first published on 29 June 2023 printed 14 January 2027. The corrigendum in OJ L 169 of 4 July 2023 changed this to 20 January 2027 ([standardsdrift.com](https://standardsdrift.com/standards/machinery-regulation/)).
- **Later amendments:** The consolidated text of 27 July 2026, which includes the amendments made by Regulations (EU) 2024/2748 and 2026/1744, still gives 20 January 2027 ([standardsdrift.com](https://standardsdrift.com/standards/machinery-regulation/)).

**Provisions that already apply**

The Regulation entered into force on 19 July 2023 ([ehsconsulting.pl](https://ehsconsulting.pl/en/machinery-regulation-2023-1230-vs-machinery-directive/)). Under Article 54, some provisions apply earlier than the general date ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02023R1230-20260529/art_54)):

- Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from 19 July 2023.
- Articles 26 to 42 from 20 January 2024.
- Article 6(2) to (6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from 20 July 2024.
- Article 50(1) from 20 October 2026.

These do not displace the Directive. Until 20 January 2027, machinery is still placed on the market under Directive 2006/42/EC, through its national transpositions.

**After the repeal**

Member States may not impede the making available of products that were placed on the market in accordance with the Directive before 20 January 2027 ([ehsconsulting.pl](https://ehsconsulting.pl/en/machinery-regulation-2023-1230-vs-machinery-directive/)).

Consolidated texts have no legal effect; the Official Journal is the authentic source ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02023R1230-20260529/art_54)).

**Last date for placing on the market or putting into service: 31 December 2028.**

Under Article 120(3a)(b) MDR, devices with a Directive 93/42/EEC certificate that remains valid by virtue of Article 120(2) may be placed on the market or put into service until 31 December 2028 where they are class IIa devices. The same date applies to class IIb devices not covered by point (a) and to class I devices that are sterile or have a measuring function ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02017R0745-20261109/art_120)). The earlier date of 31 December 2027 applies only to class III devices and most class IIb implantables.

**The two procedural deadlines under Article 120(3c)(e):**

1. **26 May 2024:** the manufacturer or its authorised representative must have lodged a formal application with a notified body for conformity assessment of the device, or of a device intended to substitute it. This is done in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII.
2. **26 September 2024:** the notified body and the manufacturer must have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02017R0745-20261109/art_120)).

Both dates have already passed, so the manufacturer can only rely on the extended period if it met them at the time. The Commission's Q&A on Regulation (EU) 2023/607 confirms that a full review of the application by the notified body was not required before the written agreement was signed ([health.ec.europa.eu](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/592008f6-3456-4afb-a13a-733a87da1b00_en)).

**Two points to check:**

- **Risk class:** for the purpose of the Article 120(3a) end date, the class is determined by the MDR's Annex VIII classification rules, not the class shown on the Directive certificate. If the device is up-classified under the MDR (for example to class III), the 31 December 2027 date would apply instead ([health.ec.europa.eu](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/592008f6-3456-4afb-a13a-733a87da1b00_en)).
- **Other 3c conditions:** these also include a further 26 May 2024 deadline, for having an MDR-compliant quality management system in place under Article 10(9). The remaining conditions are continued compliance with the Directive, no significant changes in design or intended purpose, and no unacceptable risk to health or safety ([regelex.com](https://regelex.com/legislation/02017R0745-20261109/art_120)).

In the WHO global air quality guidelines (2021 update):

- **(a) Sulfur dioxide, 24-hour mean:** 40 µg/m³
- **(b) Nitrogen dioxide, annual mean:** 10 µg/m³

For context, the SO₂ value was raised from the 2005 guideline of 20 µg/m³, while the NO₂ annual value was cut sharply from the 2005 guideline of 40 µg/m³.

**Current limit (GSR Part 3, 2014 edition):** For occupational exposure of workers over 18 years, the equivalent dose limit to the lens of the eye is 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (i.e., 100 mSv in 5 years), with no more than 50 mSv in any single year [icrp.org](https://www.icrp.org/docs/Miroslav%20Pinak%20Dose%20Limits%20to%20the%20Lens%20of%20the%20Eyes%20New%20Limit%20for%20the%20Lens%20of%20the%20Eye%20-%20International%20Basic%20Safety%20Standards%20and%20Related%20Guidance.pdf).

**Previous limit:** The preface to GSR Part 3 explains that the ICRP's April 2011 statement on tissue reactions recommended the new occupational limit, and that "previously, this dose limit had been 150 mSv per year" [nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/Set%20of%20valid%20safety%20standards%20202409/safety%20standards_%20valid%20set/GSR%20Part%203%20Radiation%20Protection%20and%20Safety%20of%20Radiation%20Sources%20International%20Basic%20Safety%20Standards.pdf). This 150 mSv per year figure was the limit in the 1996 edition of the Basic Safety Standards [journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0146645314562321).

**Context from the preface:** The Commission on Safety Standards endorsed the draft text in May 2011 but asked that Member States be consulted on the proposed lens limit. After that consultation, the Chair of the Commission approved the new limit on 12 July 2011 [nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/Set%20of%20valid%20safety%20standards%20202409/safety%20standards_%20valid%20set/GSR%20Part%203%20Radiation%20Protection%20and%20Safety%20of%20Radiation%20Sources%20International%20Basic%20Safety%20Standards.pdf). The reduction reflected ICRP's review of epidemiological evidence, which concluded that the threshold absorbed dose for the lens of the eye is now considered to be 0.5 Gy [journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0146645314562321).

**Voltage limits for scope**

Under Directive 2014/35/EU (the Low Voltage Directive), Article 1 provides that it applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of:

- **Alternating current:** between 50 and 1 000 V
- **Direct current:** between 75 and 1 500 V

other than the equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II (e.g. equipment for explosive atmospheres, radiology and medical equipment, electrical parts for lifts, electric fence controllers) [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/35/2026-05-30/eng).

The Commission's guidelines (written for the predecessor Directive 73/23/EEC and not legally binding, but the voltage limits are unchanged) clarify that these ratings refer to the voltage of the electrical input or output, not to voltages that may appear inside the equipment [webgate.ec.europa.eu](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/circabc-ewpp/rest/download/600e2761-3b06-47fa-b463-f516ee4fe7bd). Where a product has multiple voltage ratings, it falls under the Directive if the highest rating is within the limits [eurofins.com](https://www.eurofins.com/en-uk/consumer-product-testing/electrical-electronics/testing/safety-testing/low-voltage-directive-lvd/).

**Equipment designed for 24 V AC**

No. Equipment whose rated input and output voltage is 24 V AC falls below the 50 V AC lower threshold, so it is outside the scope of the Directive.

Some qualifications:

- **Accompanying power supply or charger:** If the 24 V equipment is supplied with a mains power supply unit or battery charger whose input is within the 50–1 000 V AC range, that unit is itself in scope. Likewise, equipment with an integrated power supply unit within the voltage ranges is in scope [webgate.ec.europa.eu](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/circabc-ewpp/rest/download/600e2761-3b06-47fa-b463-f516ee4fe7bd).
- **Radio equipment:** If the product contains a radio device, it falls under the Radio Equipment Directive, whose safety requirements follow LVD principles but without the lower voltage limit [eurofins.com](https://www.eurofins.com/en-uk/consumer-product-testing/electrical-electronics/testing/safety-testing/low-voltage-directive-lvd/).
- **Other legislation:** Being outside the Low Voltage Directive does not mean the product is unregulated. Other EU rules, such as general product safety legislation or other sector-specific directives, may still apply; this point goes beyond the search results provided.

Under Article 33(2) of the REACH Regulation:

- **Concentration threshold:** The duty arises when the article contains a Candidate List substance (SVHC) in a concentration **above 0.1% weight by weight (w/w)** [reachonline.eu](https://reachonline.eu/reach/en/title-iv-article-33.html).
- **Deadline:** The retailer must provide the information **within 45 days of receipt of the request** [echa.europa.eu](https://echa.europa.eu/candidate-list-obligations).
- **Charge:** No, the information must be provided **free of charge** [echa.europa.eu](https://echa.europa.eu/regulations/reach/candidate-list-substances-in-articles/communication-in-the-supply-chain).

**What must be provided:** The supplier must give the consumer sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article, including, as a minimum, the name of the substance [reachonline.eu](https://reachonline.eu/reach/en/title-iv-article-33.html).

The obligation applies to "any supplier of an article," which includes retailers, and it takes effect from the date the substance is included in the Candidate List [echa.europa.eu](https://echa.europa.eu/candidate-list-obligations).

**Trust service providers: 24 hours. Other essential and important entities: 72 hours.**

- **Trust service providers:** For significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, a trust service provider must notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority "without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident." This is a derogation from Article 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b) [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02022L2555-20221227).

- **Other essential and important entities:** Under Article 23(4)(b), the incident notification must be submitted "without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident." It updates the early warning and gives an initial assessment of the incident, including its severity and impact and, where available, indicators of compromise [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02022L2555-20221227).

A few related points:

- **Start of the clock:** Both periods run from the moment the entity becomes aware of the significant incident [ccb.belgium.be](https://ccb.belgium.be/sites/default/files/2025-08/NIS2_Notification_guide_v1.3-EN.pdf).

- **Scope of the derogation:** The 24-hour limit replaces point (b) only, and applies only to significant incidents affecting the provision of trust services [docs.modulos.ai](https://docs.modulos.ai/frameworks/nis2/incident-reporting-and-communications). Other significant incidents at a trust service provider would therefore fall under the ordinary 72-hour limit.

- **Early warning:** The separate early warning under point (a) is due within 24 hours for all entities [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02022L2555-20221227).

- **National law:** NIS2 is a directive, so these obligations apply through each Member State's transposing legislation, which is where the precise national requirements are found.

**Yes, the manufacturer must report now.** The Cyber Resilience Act's reporting obligations have applied since 11 September 2026, and they cover all products with digital elements made available in the EU, including those already on the market ([commission.europa.eu](https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/safer-and-more-secure-digital-products-2026-09-11_en)). The fact that the product was placed on the market in 2025 does not exempt it. Products placed before 11 December 2027 escape the rest of the CRA unless substantially modified from that date, but not the reporting obligations ([digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary)).

## Deadlines

The clock runs from the moment the manufacturer became aware of the active exploitation on 17 November 2026 ([enisa.europa.eu](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/media/57221)).

| Step | Deadline | In this case |
|---|---|---|
| Early warning | Within 24 hours of becoming aware | By 18 November 2026, at the same time of day awareness arose |
| Vulnerability notification | Within 72 hours of becoming aware | By 20 November 2026, at that same time of day |
| Final report | No later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available | Depends on when the patch or mitigation becomes available |

Three points on timing:

- **The early warning is due today or may already be overdue.** As of 18 November 2026, the 24-hour window is closing or has closed. If it has not been filed, the manufacturer should file it immediately.
- **The 72 hours run from awareness, not from the early warning.** Filing the early warning late does not move the second deadline.
- **Awareness means having credible information about the exploitation.** It does not mean waiting until everything is fully confirmed and documented ([cra.nbu.gov.sk](https://cra.nbu.gov.sk/en/article-14-comes-into-force-what-can-manufacturers-expect-from-11-september-2026/)).

## What to submit and where

- **Early warning:** A brief report that includes whether unlawful or deliberate action is suspected and the Member States where the product has been made available ([cra.nbu.gov.sk](https://cra.nbu.gov.sk/en/article-14-comes-into-force-what-can-manufacturers-expect-from-11-september-2026/)).
- **72-hour notification:** General information about the product, the nature of the vulnerability, and any available corrective or mitigating measures ([cra.nbu.gov.sk](https://cra.nbu.gov.sk/en/article-14-comes-into-force-what-can-manufacturers-expect-from-11-september-2026/)).
- **Where:** The manufacturer reports once through the CRA Single Reporting Platform. The notification goes to the CSIRT of the Member State of its main establishment and is made available simultaneously to ENISA, and that CSIRT then shares it with CSIRTs in the other Member States where the product is available ([digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-reporting)).

Annex II is unchanged on these points in the latest consolidation; EUR-Lex dates the current consolidated version 1 July 2026.

- **Number of substances:** Ten. These are lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE and four phthalates.
- **The 0,01 % substance:** Cadmium. The other nine all sit at 0,1 %.
- **Medical devices date:** 22 July 2021. In vitro medical devices and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial ones, share that start date.

The four phthalates (DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP) entered Annex II through Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863.

**The most they may drive in the following week is 56 hours.**

Two limits apply under Regulation (EC) No 561/2006:

1. **Two-week limit:** Total driving time in any two consecutive weeks must not exceed 90 hours ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02006R0561-20240522)). Having driven 30 hours, this alone would allow 90 − 30 = 60 hours.

2. **Weekly limit:** Weekly driving time must not exceed 56 hours ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02006R0561-20240522)). This is lower than 60, so it is the binding limit.

The total over the two weeks would then be 86 hours, which is within the 90-hour cap.

A few practical points:

- **Daily limits still apply.** Driving is limited to 9 hours a day, extendable to 10 hours twice a week ([transport.ec.europa.eu](https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-modes/road/social-provisions/driving-time-and-rest-periods_en)).
- **The week after is affected.** Driving 56 hours in one week leaves a maximum of 34 hours for the next ([onlinevrachtwagentheorie.nl](https://onlinevrachtwagentheorie.nl/en/rijtijden-calculator)).
- **Working time rules also count.** Weekly driving must not cause the maximum weekly working time in Directive 2002/15/EC to be exceeded ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A02006R0561-20240522)). Working time includes loading, unloading, cleaning and maintenance, and administrative formalities ([europa.eu](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/work/work-abroad/rules-working-road-transport/index_en.htm)).
- **There is a narrow exception.** In exceptional circumstances, a driver may exceed the daily and weekly driving time by up to one hour to reach home or the employer's operational centre for a weekly rest, or by up to two hours for a regular weekly rest ([transport.ec.europa.eu](https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-modes/road/social-provisions/driving-time-and-rest-periods_en)).

**Answer: (a) 200 kΩ; (b) 40 kΩ**

This falls under paragraph 5.1.3.2 (electric power train consisting of combined DC- and AC-buses), which applies when the AC and DC high voltage buses are galvanically connected.

**(a) No additional AC protection: 200 kΩ**

The isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis must be at least 500 Ω per volt of working voltage [unece.org](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/GRSP-79-14.pdf).

500 Ω/V × 400 V = 200,000 Ω = 200 kΩ

**(b) All AC buses protected by one of the two listed measures: 40 kΩ**

The minimum drops to 100 Ω per volt of working voltage if all AC high voltage buses are protected by either of the following [unece.org](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/GRSP-79-14.pdf):

- Two or more layers of solid insulators, electrical protection barriers or enclosures that each independently meet paragraph 5.1.1 (for example, wiring harness).
- Mechanically robust protections with sufficient durability over the vehicle's service life, such as motor housings, electronic converter cases or connectors.

100 Ω/V × 400 V = 40,000 Ω = 40 kΩ

**Notes**

- **Source version:** The search results confirm the 2026/1695 publication exists ([op.europa.eu](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/00a89d2d-99d5-11f1-9262-01aa75ed71a1/language-en)) but do not include its text. The wording above comes from a 2026 UNECE working document consolidating the 05 series, and it is identical to the 03 series text published in the Official Journal ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A42021X2190)).
- **Working voltage:** This is the highest rms voltage specified by the manufacturer that may occur in open circuit or normal operating conditions [unece.org](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/GRSP-79-14.pdf), so the 400 V figure should be that value.
- **Demonstrating compliance:** The isolation resistance may be shown by calculation, measurement or a combination of both, with measurement carried out according to Annex 5A [unece.org](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/GRSP-79-14.pdf).

**TI = 16, which is within the limit of 50 for a freight container used as packaging under SSR-6 (Rev. 2).**

The current edition is IAEA SSR-6 (Rev. 2); the 2018 edition now carries a notice that Rev. 2 has replaced it.

**Calculation (para. 523)**

1. Dose rate at 1 m: 0.08 mSv/h × 100 = 8. The factor of 100 is the first step of the procedure.
2. Load-size factor: a Table 7 factor is then applied in Rev. 2 where a tank or freight container serves as the packaging. A 3 m² cross-section falls in the "more than 1 m² up to 5 m²" band, which carries a factor of 2. The search results confirm the band but not the factor itself; the value of 2 is from my knowledge of Table 7.
3. 8 × 2 = 16. Rounding up to one decimal place is the final step, and it changes nothing here.

**Limit check (para. 526)**

Rev. 2 sets a separate ceiling of 50 on the TI when a freight container is itself the packaging. A TI of 16 is below 50, so the container complies without exclusive use.

This is a change from the 2018 edition (Rev. 1). From my recollection of that edition, a freight container used as packaging fell under the general package limit of TI 10 unless shipped under exclusive use, so a TI of 16 would have required exclusive use.

There is no employee threshold. The GDPR does not make a data protection officer (DPO) mandatory at any particular headcount.

Under Article 37(1), a controller or processor must designate a DPO in three alternative cases, none of which depends on size ([complyfine.com](https://www.complyfine.com/gdpr-compliance/gdpr-article-37-dpo)):

- **Public authorities:** the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except courts acting in their judicial capacity.
- **Large-scale monitoring:** the organisation's core activities require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale.
- **Large-scale sensitive data:** the organisation's core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data (Article 9) or data on criminal convictions and offences (Article 10).

So a small company can be caught and a large one can fall outside. The European Commission lists "a small head-hunting company that profiles individuals" as an example where a DPO is mandatory ([commission.europa.eu](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/obligations_en)).

**Where the "250 employees" idea comes from**

- An early draft of the GDPR limited mandatory DPO appointments to companies with more than 250 employees, but the final version dropped that threshold ([lexgo.lu](https://www.lexgo.lu/en/news-and-articles/4434-gdpr-n-5-new-data-protection-obligations)).
- The figure of 250 does appear in Article 30(5), but that is a partial exemption from the record-keeping duty and has nothing to do with DPOs ([complyfine.com](https://www.complyfine.com/gdpr-compliance/gdpr-article-37-dpo)).

**National law can differ**

Article 37(4) lets EU or Member State law require a DPO in additional cases. Germany has done so, which is why a headcount rule does apply to some controllers there, though not under the GDPR itself ([complyfine.com](https://www.complyfine.com/gdpr-compliance/gdpr-article-37-dpo)).

**No — the insulin pump is exempt from those requirements.**

**Applicability to the insulin pump**

Article 2(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 provides that, by way of derogation from Article 1, the essential requirements in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU "shall not apply to radio equipment to which either of the following Union legislation also applies: (a) Regulation (EU) 2017/745; (b) Regulation (EU) 2017/746" ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R0030)). Since the pump is a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, none of the three cybersecurity requirements (network protection, personal data/privacy safeguards, fraud protection) apply to it.

The rationale, in recital 15, is that the medical device regulations already address certain elements of the cybersecurity risks covered by Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f) ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R0030)). The UK government factsheet confirms the same reading ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/radio-equipment-regulations-2017/regulation-eu-202230-factsheet)).

The exemption is limited to these cybersecurity requirements. The pump remains radio equipment, so the other requirements of the Radio Equipment Directive still apply, and its cybersecurity is governed by the Medical Devices Regulation.

**Date of application for equipment that is covered**

- **1 August 2025.** The Regulation as originally published set 1 August 2024 ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R0030)), but Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 amended Article 3 to read "It shall apply from 1 August 2025" ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ%3AL_202302444)).
- **Repeal ahead:** Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/339, published on 29 April 2026, repeals Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 with effect from 11 December 2027, when the main obligations of the Cyber Resilience Act begin to apply ([single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/radio-equipment-directive-red_en)). The requirements therefore apply to covered equipment from 1 August 2025 until that date.

- **Level AA criterion:** Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), which is new in WCAG 2.2 [w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/).
- **Minimum size:** Targets for pointer inputs must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, subject to exceptions (spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control, essential) [w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum).
- **Spacing exception circle:** Undersized targets can still pass if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle centered on each one's bounding box does not intersect another target or the circle of another undersized target [w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum).
- **Level AAA size:** Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) requires at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels [w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-enhanced). The spacing exception does not apply to this enhanced criterion [ta11y.org](https://www.ta11y.org/en/learning/web/pointer/target-size/).

**No.** The Recommendation published on 12 December 2024 is WCAG 2.2, and it has removed success criterion 4.1.1 Parsing, so it is not a requirement for Level A or AA conformance to that version ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)). The criterion appears in the document only as "Parsing (Obsolete and removed)".

**The stated reason** is given in the note under that heading ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)):

> "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."

W3C's supporting material adds that browsers and specifications such as HTML now handle parsing errors better, and assistive technology relies on the browser rather than parsing markup itself ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/)). Accessibility problems that would have failed 4.1.1 now fail other criteria, such as 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/parsing)).

**For the questionnaire:**

- **Suggested answer:** A pass/fail result doesn't fit WCAG 2.2. The accurate response is "Not applicable: 4.1.1 is obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2."
- **If WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 also applies:** WCAG 2.2 notes that authors required by policy to conform to those versions "may need to continue to test and report 4.1.1" ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)). Even there, W3C has added a note that the criterion "should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML" ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/)).
- **Still covered elsewhere:** Markup defects that actually affect users, such as duplicate IDs that break label or ARIA references, should be reported under 1.3.1 or 4.1.2.

Per FIPS 197:

- **Rounds:** AES-256 uses **14 rounds** (Nr = 14).
- **Block size:** **128 bits** (Nb = 4 words of 32 bits each), the same for all AES variants.
- **Round keys:** The cipher consumes **15 round keys** (Nr + 1), each consisting of four 32-bit words (128 bits). That's one for the initial AddRoundKey, plus one for each of the 14 rounds.

The key expansion therefore produces 4 × (Nr + 1) = **60 words** in total from the 256-bit (Nk = 8 words) cipher key.

Under NIST SP 800-38D (November 2007), for AES-GCM with RBG-based IVs:

**1. Recommended IV length: 96 bits (12 bytes)**
The standard recommends that implementations restrict support to 96-bit IVs "to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design" ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/legacy/sp/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf)). This is a recommendation ("it is recommended"), not a mandatory "shall." It is consistent with the RBG-based construction in Sec. 8.2.2, which requires the random field to be at least 96 bits and recommends the free field be empty, so that the random field is the entire IV ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.800-38d)).

**2. Maximum invocations per key: 2^32 (4,294,967,296)**
Sec. 8.3 states that for the RBG-based construction, with IVs of any length, "the total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key" ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/legacy/sp/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf)). This is a global limit: it covers every device or instance sharing the key, not each one separately. Combined with the 96-bit minimum random field, it ensures the Sec. 8 uniqueness requirement, that the probability of an IV repeating under one key is no greater than 2^-32.

**3. Maximum plaintext per invocation: 2^36 − 32 bytes (68,719,476,704 bytes)**
The standard states the limit in bits: len(P) ≤ 2^39 − 256 ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/legacy/sp/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf)). Dividing by 8 gives 2^36 − 32 bytes, just under 64 GiB, which matches the byte figure given in the AES-GCM CAESAR baseline submission ([competitions.cr.yp.to](https://competitions.cr.yp.to/baseline/gcmsub.pdf)).

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 does not require any specific number, time period, or lockout duration. All three values are organization-defined parameters.

**What the control actually says**

Per the control statement at [csf.tools](https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/ac/ac-7/), organizations must:

1. Enforce a limit of *[organization-defined number]* consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during an *[organization-defined time period]*; and
2. Automatically take one or more of the following actions when that maximum is exceeded:
   - lock the account or node for an *[organization-defined time period]*
   - lock the account or node until released by an administrator
   - delay the next logon prompt per an *[organization-defined delay algorithm]*
   - notify the system administrator
   - take other *[organization-defined action]*

So a timed lockout is itself only one of several permissible responses.

**Why the values are blank**

The publication explains that assignment operations let organizations customize controls based on their security and privacy requirements, drawing on laws, regulations, policies, risk assessments, and risk tolerance. Once specified by the organization, the values become part of the control, and implementation is assessed against the completed control statement ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf)).

**Typical values in practice**

- **Common industry practice:** three to five consecutive failed attempts within a 15- to 30-minute window, with a temporary lockout of 15 to 30 minutes ([upguard.com](https://www.upguard.com/compliance/nist-sp-800-53/ac/ac-7)).
- **U.S. Department of Education:** three consecutive invalid attempts in a 30-minute period, with a 30-minute lockout. The account is disabled until an administrator re-enables it after three consecutive lockouts ([ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/fund/contract/about/acs/2022-ac-access-control-standard-signed.pdf)).
- **Maryland State Department of Education:** three consecutive invalid attempts in a 15-minute period, with a 30-minute lockout ([oit.msde.maryland.gov](https://oit.msde.maryland.gov/Content/Uploads/Policy/IT%20Security%20Policy/Access%20Control_2024.pdf)).

If you need to meet a specific requirement, the binding values will come from your organization's policy or an applicable overlay or baseline, not from SP 800-53 itself.

**Current revision (Revision 3, May 2024): 17 families.** The document states that "the security requirements are organized into 17 families" ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r3.pdf)).

**Revision 2: 14 families.** The search results don't state this number directly, but it follows from NIST's FAQ, which says three new families were added in Revision 3: Planning (PL), System and Services Acquisition (SA), and Supply Chain Risk Management (SR) ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/Projects/protecting-controlled-unclassified-information/documents/FAQ/FAQ-SP800-171R3-171AR3.pdf)). The FAQ also notes that the Security Assessment family was renamed Security Assessment and Monitoring (CA), which did not change the count.

**Revision 2's status: superseded.** Revision 3's publication history reads "Supersedes NIST Special Publication 800-171r2 (February 2020; Includes updates as of 01-28-2021)" ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r3.pdf)). The search results don't include NIST's copy of Revision 2 itself. From my recollection, that PDF carries a cover notice marking it as a withdrawn publication, superseded by Revision 3 on May 14, 2024, but I can't confirm that from these sources.

Superseded does not mean irrelevant: NIST's small business primer notes that the Department of Defense's CMMC program "is currently based on SP 800-171, Revision 2," and that contractors should check their contracts for the version they must use ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.1318.pdf)).

**Yes, checksums are enabled.** Starting with PostgreSQL 18, `initdb` turns on data checksums by default, so a cluster created with no checksum-related option has them on. (In version 17 and earlier, the default was off and you had to pass `--data-checksums` / `-k`.) This is from my own knowledge of the PostgreSQL 18 release, not a fresh search.

**Switching them off:**

- **At creation time:** run `initdb --no-data-checksums`, an option added in version 18.
- **On an existing cluster:** shut the server down cleanly and run `pg_checksums --disable -D <datadir>`. This works offline only; `pg_checksums --enable` reverses it.

You can check the current state with `SHOW data_checksums;` or `pg_controldata`.

**Requirement for pg_upgrade:** the old and new clusters must have the same checksum setting, either both on or both off. `pg_upgrade` refuses to proceed on a mismatch.

This matters in version 18 because most older clusters were created without checksums, while a default new cluster has them. When upgrading such a cluster, either:

- create the new cluster with `initdb --no-data-checksums` to match the old one, or
- enable checksums on the old cluster first with `pg_checksums --enable` (offline, and it rewrites every data block, so allow time for large databases).

On a current Linux kernel:

- **Range:** `vm.swappiness` accepts values from **0 to 200** ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html?highlight=swappiness)). The upper limit was raised from 100 to 200 in kernel 5.8; on older kernels, writing a value above 100 fails with an "Invalid argument" error ([linuxize.com](https://linuxize.com/post/how-to-change-the-swappiness-value-in-linux/)).

- **Default:** **60** ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html?highlight=swappiness)).

- **Swap 2x faster than filesystem IO:** **133**. The kernel documentation gives this exact example: if random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33) ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html?highlight=swappiness)).

The value is not a percentage. It expresses the relative IO cost of swapping versus filesystem paging. At 100, the kernel assumes the two cost the same; lower values mean swap is more expensive, and higher values mean it is cheaper ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html?highlight=swappiness)). That is why values above 100 can suit in-memory swap such as zram or zswap.

To try the value without making it persistent:

```bash
sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=133
```

This lasts until the next reboot ([linuxize.com](https://linuxize.com/post/how-to-change-the-swappiness-value-in-linux/)). The kernel docs note that the optimal value is workload-dependent and requires experimentation, so 133 is a starting point ([kernel.org](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html?highlight=swappiness)).

**Current default on Linux (3.15 series): `forkserver`.** According to the documentation, forkserver is available on POSIX platforms that support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes, such as Linux, and is the default on those platforms [docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html).

**Default before Python 3.14: `fork`.** The docs note that in 3.14 "the default start method was changed from fork to forkserver to retain the performance but avoid common multithreaded process incompatibilities" (gh-84559), and that fork "is no longer the default start method on any platform". Code that needs fork must request it explicitly via `get_context()` or `set_start_method()` [docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html). This change was flagged in advance in the deprecation notes [docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3/deprecations/pending-removal-in-3.14.html).

**When the default becomes `spawn` instead:** when there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires, for example on a read-only file system. Per the docs, this changed in version 3.15.1; previously forkserver remained the default in that situation and starting a process failed with an `OSError` [docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html).

Related details:

- **The default is determined lazily.** The docs state the default "is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported" [docs.python.org](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html). The associated backport PR explains that this happens on the first `get_context()`, `get_start_method()`, `get_all_start_methods()` or default `Process` start, and that it was done to avoid slowing down `import multiprocessing` [github.com](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/159271). That PR is listed as open in the search result, although the docs already describe the behavior.
- **How writability is checked.** The implementation actually tries to create a temporary file rather than relying on `os.access()`, which its comments call "advisory and racy". It also returns false, leading to spawn, if no usable temporary directory exists at all [github.com](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/util.py).

With kube-apiserver at v1.27, only the v1.25 kubelet is inside the supported skew.

- **v1.28 – not supported.** The kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver ([kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/)).
- **v1.25 – supported.** It is two minor versions older than the API server, which is within the limit under both the old and the current rule.
- **v1.24 – not supported.** It is three minor versions older, and the three-version allowance does not apply here: kubelets older than 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver ([kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/)).

The three-version skew was introduced starting with v1.25 nodes and v1.28 control planes ([kubernetes.dev](https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3935/)). The same proposal notes that v1.27 control planes were not fully compatible with v1.24 nodes, for example because of the removal of in-tree volume plugin support that relies on kubelet behaviour only guaranteed in v1.25+.

Specific deployment tools or managed services may place additional restrictions on version skew beyond the upstream policy.

The node port is allocated from the default range **30000-32767**, which is what the control plane uses when `--service-node-port-range` is not set [kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/). The range is inclusive at both ends [kubernetes.dev](https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3668/).

**Band split under the default range**

- **Static band:** 30000-30085 (86 ports)
- **Dynamic band:** 30086-32767 (2,682 ports)

[kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

**How the split is calculated**

The static band size comes from the formula `min(max(16, nodeport-size / 32), 128)`. For the default range of 2,768 ports, that gives `min(max(16, 86), 128)` = 86 [kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/05/11/nodeport-dynamic-and-static-allocation/).

**What this means for the operator's Service**

Because `nodePort` was not set, the port is assigned dynamically. Dynamic assignment uses the upper band (30086-32767) by default, and falls back to the lower band only once the upper band is exhausted [kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/). So in practice the Service will get a port in 30086-32767 unless that band is full.

The lower band is intended for users who manually pick a port, which lowers the risk of collision with dynamically assigned ports [kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/05/11/nodeport-dynamic-and-static-allocation/).

**Version note**

This banding behaviour is tied to the `ServiceNodePortStaticSubrange` feature, which was alpha in v1.27, beta in v1.28 and stable in v1.29 [kubernetes.dev](https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3668/). On older clusters without it, dynamic ports are drawn from the whole 30000-32767 range.

In the WebAssembly 3.0 core specification:

- **Page size:** 65,536 bytes (64 KiB, i.e. 2^16 bytes).
- **i32 memories:** at most 2^16 = 65,536 pages, which is 2^32 bytes = 4,294,967,296 bytes (4 GiB).
- **i64 memories:** at most 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages, which corresponds to 2^64 bytes (16 EiB).

Both limits come from the same validation rule: a memory type's limits must fall within 2^(N−16) pages, where N is the bit width of the address type. That is the full address space divided by the page size.

These are validation limits only; an engine may fail to allocate or grow a memory well below them. This answer is from memory of the spec rather than a fresh lookup.

**Level 3:** The recommended range for a WebAuthn ceremony timeout is 300000 to 600000 milliseconds, with a recommended default of 300000 milliseconds (5 minutes), as summarised by [corbado.com](https://www.corbado.com/glossary/publickeycredentialrequestoptions). The Level 3 excerpt I have doesn't show the numbers itself; it only points to a single "recommended range and default for a WebAuthn ceremony timeout" ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/)).

**Level 2:** The recommendation depended on the `userVerification` setting ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/)):

| `userVerification` | Recommended range | Recommended default |
|---|---|---|
| `discouraged` | 30000 to 180000 ms | 120000 ms (2 minutes) |
| `required` or `preferred` | 30000 to 600000 ms | 300000 ms (5 minutes) |

So when `userVerification` is `discouraged`, Level 2 recommended a shorter window: 30000 to 180000 ms with a 120000 ms default. Level 3 instead gives a single recommendation, with a higher minimum (300000 ms) and a longer default (5 minutes rather than 2).

Browsers treat the timeout as a hint and may clamp or override it, and their own defaults vary widely ([satragno.com](https://satragno.com/blog/webauthn-timeout/)).

Under RFC 9293, Section 3.7.1, if no MSS Option is received at connection setup, a TCP implementation **MUST** assume a default send MSS of:

- **IPv4:** 536 bytes (576 − 40)
- **IPv6:** 1220 bytes (1280 − 60)

This is a **MUST**-level (mandatory) requirement, labeled **MUST-15** in the RFC's requirement numbering scheme [ietf.lantern.io](https://ietf.lantern.io/rfcs/rfc-9293). The RFC's wording is: "If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15)" [networkengineering.stackexchange.com](https://networkengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/85929/mtu-and-mss-concept).

Some additional context:

- **Where the numbers come from:** These defaults derive from minimum receive assumptions, not typical Ethernet MTUs [harshvermac5.github.io](https://harshvermac5.github.io/learn/2026/tcp-mss-mtu-path-mtu/). The arithmetic in the RFC subtracts 40 bytes of headers from 576 for IPv4, and 60 bytes from 1280 for IPv6.
- **History:** The IPv4 default was carried over from RFC 1122, Section 4.2.2.6, which stated that TCP MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 − 40) when no MSS option is received [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6691.html). RFC 9293 adds the IPv6 value alongside it.
- **Related requirements:** Endpoints MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option (MUST-14). They SHOULD send an MSS Option in every SYN segment when their receive MSS differs from the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6 (SHLD-5), and MAY send it always (MAY-3) [github.com](https://github.com/shuji-bonji/rfcxml-mcp/blob/master/examples/rfc9293-tcp-checklist.md).

**(a) Canada – 1.0 mW/cm².** Under Part III of the Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, leakage radiation at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface must not exceed 1.0 mW/cm² with the prescribed test load in place. For a domestic cooking oven of no more than 1.5 kW, that load is 275 ± 15 ml of water placed in the centre of the shelf in the cavity [laws-lois.justice.gc.ca](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/C.R.C.,_c._1370/FullText.html?wbdisable=true).

**(b) United States, before acquisition by a purchaser – 1 mW/cm².** Under 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), the equivalent plane-wave power density must not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimetre at any point 5 cm or more from the external surface, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-J/part-1030/section-1030.10).

**(c) United States, after acquisition – 5 mW/cm².** The same paragraph sets the limit thereafter at 5 milliwatts per square centimetre at any such point [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-J/part-1030/section-1030.10). The FDA summarises this as 1 mW per sq cm prior to purchase and 5 mW per sq cm throughout useful life [fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/radiation-emitting-products/laws-and-regulations-radiation-emitting-products/summary-electronic-product-radiation-control-provisions-federal-food-drug-and-cosmetic-fdc-act).

Two related points:

- **The Canadian 5.0 mW/cm² figure is not a post-sale limit.** It applies to operation without a test load, where the oven can operate that way [laws-lois.justice.gc.ca](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/C.R.C.,_c._1370/FullText.html?wbdisable=true). Health Canada notes that after-sale (used) ovens are not covered by these regulations [canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/environmental-workplace-health/reports-publications/radiation/radiation-leakage-before-sale-used-microwave-ovens-health-canada-2000.html).
- **The test load is the same in both countries.** The US standard also specifies 275 ± 15 ml of water at 20 ± 5 °C, with the oven at maximum output [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-J/part-1030/section-1030.10).

**2.0 hours per employee per 24-hour period at 93 dBA, and a separate L(ex,8) ceiling of 87 dBA.**

- **Duration limit at 93 dBA:** The schedule to section 7.4 pairs 93 dBA with 2.0 hours per employee per 24-hour period.
- **L(ex,8) ceiling:** Section 7.4(b) caps the 8-hour-normalised noise exposure level at 87 dBA.

An amendment was proposed in the Canada Gazette, Part I, on 21 March 2026 that would lower the federal limits. That notice still describes 87 dBA as the current maximum, and I did not find confirmation that the change has been finalised, so check the current consolidated text on the Justice Laws site if this is for compliance purposes.

- **Maximum EIRP:** 4 W. Digital modulation transmitters in 2400–2483.5 MHz carry a 4 W ceiling, with further conditions set out in clause 43.
- **Additional limit:** Operation is barred where radiated peak power spectral density goes above 25 mW per 3 kHz.
- **Year made:** 2025. The instrument in force is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025. ACMA decided to make it after consultation, with a 1 October 2025 start date, and the 2015 licence it replaced was scheduled to sunset that same day.

Two caveats:

- The 4 W and 25 mW per 3 kHz figures come from ACMA's March 2025 consultation draft, not the registered text. They match the 2015 licence's long-standing limits, but I did not open the final version on the Federal Register of Legislation.
- I did not check whether the 2025 licence has been varied since commencement, so confirm against the current compilation on the Register if this is for compliance.

The older licence also required a minimum 6 dB bandwidth of at least 500 kHz for this class. I could not confirm from the search results whether clause 43 of the 2025 instrument retains that condition.

**Exposure limit values**

Under regulation 4(3) of the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, the exposure limit values are:

- **Daily or weekly personal noise exposure:** 87 dB(A)
- **Peak sound pressure:** 140 dB(C)

These are set out in the Regulations at [legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4), and the HSE describes them as levels of exposure which must not be exceeded ([hse.gov.uk](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/employers.htm)).

**Counting hearing protector attenuation**

No, the attenuation of hearing protectors cannot be counted when judging whether the upper exposure action value has been reached.

Regulation 4(5) allows the protection given by employer-provided hearing protectors to be taken into account only when applying the exposure limit values. It expressly excludes the lower and upper exposure action values ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4)). This mirrors the underlying EU Directive 2003/10/EC, which says the action values "shall not take account of the effect of any such protectors" ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2003/10/article/3/data.html)).

**What this means in practice**

- **Upper exposure action values:** 85 dB(A) daily or weekly exposure and 137 dB(C) peak. These are assessed on the noise the employee is actually exposed to, ignoring any hearing protection.
- **Exposure limit values:** 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C). These are assessed on exposure at the ear, so the attenuation of protectors issued under regulation 7(2) can be counted.
- **Weekly averaging:** weekly exposure may be used in place of daily exposure where exposure varies markedly from day to day (regulation 4(4)).

Staying below the limit value with hearing protection does not remove the duty under regulation 6 to eliminate or reduce noise at source so far as is reasonably practicable ([noiseregulationsuk.co.uk](https://noiseregulationsuk.co.uk/legislation/exposure-limit-values/)). That page attributes the limit value to regulation 4(2), but the official text places it in regulation 4(3); 4(2) contains the upper exposure action values.

This is general information rather than legal advice.

**Standard carbon monoxide limits (EH40/2005, fourth edition 2020, Table 1):**

- Long-term (8-hour TWA): **20 ppm** (23 mg/m³)
- Short-term (15-minute): **100 ppm** (117 mg/m³)

These figures appear in Table 1 of EH40 itself ([hse.gov.uk](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/priced/eh40.pdf)).

**Does the higher pair still apply on 17 November 2026?**

No, going by the wording of Table 1. The higher pair was a transitional allowance for underground mining and tunnelling that ran out on 21 August 2023, more than three years ago. On that reading, the 20 ppm and 100 ppm limits now apply to all industries, including mining and tunnelling.

The fourth edition (2020) was still listed as HSE's current edition as of 5 October 2026 ([unibuild.co.uk](https://unibuild.co.uk/coshh/workplace-exposure-limits/)). If you work in those sectors, check HSE's current workplace exposure limits page for any update.

**(a) Sprinkler threshold:** A sprinkler system throughout the building, in accordance with Appendix E, is recommended once a block of flats has a top storey more than 11m above ground level (paragraph 7.4).

NASA-STD-4003A sets no maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R joint, so the question rests on a limit that isn't in the standard. What it imposes instead is a qualitative RF design requirement plus a DC resistance limit.

- **RF requirement (qualitative):** Inductance and overall impedance of the bond path and its joints, resonances included, must be kept low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest. The designer decides what those frequencies are and what "low enough" means for the system.
- **Numerical requirement (DC only):** Each joint in the path is limited to 2.5 milliohms of DC resistance.

The standard's own guidance section is candid about the limits of that number:

- The 2.5-milliohm figure is historical and has no RF design basis; its purpose is to confirm good metal-to-metal contact.
- An acceptable bond can sit in the ohms range at RF while still measuring under 2.5 milliohms at DC.
- Passing the DC measurement is not proof of a good RF bond; the standard warns that "good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms" is not a safe assumption.
- Where bond straps cannot be avoided, the guidance recommends a length-to-width ratio of no more than 5 to 1. That wording comes from a NASA Goddard presentation quoting the original NASA-STD-4003, not from the 4003A text itself.

In practice, the designer should verify each joint against the 2.5-milliohm DC limit, then show by design that the path is low-inductance at the system's frequencies of interest. Direct, short, wide metal-to-metal contact is the usual way to do that.

The requirement wording I could retrieve came from the historical 4003A release. The current edition is 4003A with Change 1, which numbers this requirement [EBR 21], so check the exact text there before quoting it in a compliance document.

According to NOAA CO-OPS:

- **Current epoch:** Official U.S. tidal datums are currently based on the 1983–2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch ([tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html)).
- **Replacement (fifth) epoch:** The update will be based on water level data spanning 2002–2020 ([tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html)).
- **Proposed release year:** New NTDE products are currently proposed for release in 2029. The updated datums and bench mark sheets for all roughly 2,000 stations are to be released simultaneously that year ([tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/faq.html)).

The CO-OPS Datum Calculator adds that the official release is planned for early 2029, and that any 2002–2020 datums computed before then are preliminary, unofficial, and for planning purposes only ([access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov](https://access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov/datumcalc/)).

**Buffer interval minimum (11th Edition):** At least 2 seconds. Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 (a Standard) says that after the pedestrian change interval, "a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement" ([buildspec.codes](https://buildspec.codes/codes/mutcd/4i.06)).

**Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time:** 3.5 feet per second. Paragraph 07 (Guidance) says the clearance time should let a pedestrian who left the curb at the end of the WALK indication reach at least the far side of the traveled way, or a median wide enough to wait on, at that speed ([mutcd.fyi](https://www.mutcd.fyi/11r1/part-4i-pedestrian-control-features/)).

Two provisions adjust this default:
- **Faster:** Up to 4 feet per second may be used where an extended push button press function lets slower pedestrians request more time ([up.codes](https://up.codes/s/pedestrian-intervals-and-signal-phases)).
- **Slower:** A speed below 3.5 feet per second should be considered where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk ([buildspec.codes](https://buildspec.codes/codes/mutcd/4i.06)).

**Buffer interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD:** At least 3 seconds. The search results provided don't cover the 2009 edition, so this comes from my own knowledge of it: the equivalent provision was Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04. The 11th Edition therefore reduced the minimum from 3 seconds to 2 seconds. You can verify this against the 2009 text on FHWA's MUTCD site.

**The two capacity ceilings (SPCC rule, 40 CFR Part 112)**

To fall outside the rule on capacity grounds, the facility must meet both of these limits:

- **Aboveground:** aggregate storage capacity of **1,320 US gallons or less** of oil.
- **Completely buried:** storage capacity of **42,000 US gallons or less** of oil.

The exemption requires both conditions to be met, so exceeding either one brings the facility under the rule ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-112)).

**Which aboveground containers count**

- Only containers with a capacity of **55 US gallons or greater** are counted ([law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/112.1)). A standard 55-gallon drum therefore counts.
- Use the container's **shell capacity** (maximum volume), not the amount of oil actually in it ([epa.gov](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/spccbluebroch.pdf)).
- Counted containers include aboveground tanks (shop-built or field-erected) and mobile or portable containers such as drums, totes, non-transportation-related tank trucks and mobile refuelers ([epa.gov](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/spccbluebroch.pdf)).
- Bunkered tanks, partially buried tanks and containers in vaults are treated as aboveground containers ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-112)).

**Excluded from the aboveground total** ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-112)):

- Permanently closed containers
- Motive power containers
- Hot-mix asphalt and its containers
- Heating oil containers used solely at a single-family residence
- Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers
- Milk and milk product containers and associated piping

EPA's applicability checklist also excludes containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment ([epa.gov](https://www.epa.gov/oil-spills-prevention-and-preparedness-regulations/does-spill-prevention-control-and-countermeasure)).

**Notes on the buried total**

The 42,000-gallon figure excludes completely buried tanks subject to all the technical requirements of the underground storage tank rules (40 CFR Part 280 or an approved state program under Part 281), as well as permanently closed tanks ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-112)).

Separately from capacity, a facility is also outside the rule if, based on its location alone, it could not reasonably be expected to discharge oil into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. That determination must ignore manmade features such as dikes ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-112)).

**10 TR ≈ 35.17 kW**

**Calculation:**

- NIST SP 811 (Appendix B.8) lists the ton of refrigeration as 12 000 Btu_IT/h, which gives 1 TR = 3516.8528 W ≈ 3.516853 kW ([scientificconverters.com](https://scientificconverters.com/power/tons-of-refrigeration-to-kilowatts/), [formula.expert](https://formula.expert/constants/ton-of-refrigeration)).
- 10 TR × 3.516853 kW/TR = 35.16853 kW
- Rounded to four significant figures: **35.17 kW**

This matches the published conversion table value of 10 TR = 35.16852842 kW ([scientificconverters.com](https://scientificconverters.com/power/tons-of-refrigeration-to-kilowatts/)), and the factor is exact by definition because the International Table Btu is exactly defined ([formula.expert](https://formula.expert/constants/ton-of-refrigeration)).

Note that this is the chiller's heat-removal rate (cooling capacity), not its electrical input power ([globalcalcs.com](https://globalcalcs.com/en/conversion/refrigeration-ton-converter/)).

**Datasheet values (Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24):**

- **Maximum power dissipation at TC = 25 °C:** 130 W
- **Linear derating factor:** 0.87 W/°C

Both figures appear in the Absolute Maximum Ratings table of the Infineon datasheet [infineon.com](https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-irf540npbf-datasheet-en.pdf), and are echoed by third-party summaries of Rev. 2.1 [partvane.com](https://www.partvane.com/parts/infineon/irf540npbf/), [sourceics.com](https://sourceics.com/parts/IRF540NPBF).

**Derated power at TC = 100 °C:**

PD(100 °C) = 130 W − 0.87 W/°C × (100 − 25) °C
= 130 W − 65.25 W
= **64.75 W (≈ 65 W)**

**Cross-check:** The derating factor is the reciprocal of the junction-to-case thermal resistance (1 ÷ 1.15 °C/W ≈ 0.87 W/°C), and the 130 W rating corresponds to (175 − 25) °C ÷ 1.15 °C/W [cnfx.com](https://cnfx.com/industry/computer-electronic-and-optical-product-manufacturing/product/active-device). Using the thermal resistance directly, (175 − 100) ÷ 1.15 ≈ 65.2 W, which agrees with the derating result; the small difference comes from rounding of the 0.87 figure.

Note that this is a calculated value, not one stated in the datasheet, and it assumes the case is actually held at 100 °C. In a real design, the case-to-sink and sink-to-ambient resistances reduce the usable dissipation further.
